newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asia Grain - Japan still not tempted by China corn.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Grain - Japan still not tempted by China corn.

text.p: Chinese sellers continue to offer corn to Japan but their offers still remain uncompetitive versus U.S. origin, Tokyo traders said on Monday.
Chinese corn is now being offered at about $130 a tonne CIF from Dalian port on China's northeast coast, they said.
"The freight between Dalian and Japan costs about $20 (a tonne). The total cost is not competitive against U.S.," one corn trader said.

A trader in Hong Kong who represents China's central food trading arm China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import Export Corp (COFCO), said A 1994 Chinese export ban on corn had been lifted and exports this year could be one million tonnes.
This could not be immediately confirmed with COFCO.
Despite the reported Japanese offers, the trader said COFCO officials were keen to maintain a Dalian FOB price of $135 a tonne, now a good $7 higher than the international market.
Japanese traders said they are continuing to buy U.S. corn for April-June shipment and have so far covered up to 40 percent of their requirements for the second quarter of this year.
Premiums for U.S. corn were quoted at between 95 and 96 U.S. cents a bushel over the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) May contract, they said.

"Freight rates have moved upwards since late last week, probably because of stable vessel demand from the steel industry. U.S. premiums (over CBOT futures) will be raised later this week in line with the freight rate," one corn trader said.

In South Korea, several purchasing groups are likely to buy up to four 50,000-tonne cargoes of corn this week for shipment between April and May, but others are expected to hold back ahead of the Lunar New Year holiday on Friday, traders said.
They said said there was talk in the market of sellers being unwilling to offer corn for the April/May period because they expect strong demand from Asian countries to push prices higher.

"Some (South Korean) buyers are trying to buy corn soon for shipment in April and May ahead of other Asian buyers," one trader said. He said most corn from this period will be shipped from the Argentine new crop.
"We have bought corn in January. It is enough to cover some of our requirements for the second quarter," an official with a local feed milling company said.
The official said most South Korean companies were expected to resume their corn purchases after the national holiday.

A trader with the National Livestock Cooperative Federation (NLCF) said freight rates from the U.S. Pacific Northwest to South Korea have fallen slightly to between $12 to $12.50 a tonne from $12.50 to $13 a week ago. Rates from the U.S. Gulf have also eased by 50 U.S. cents a tonne to $22 to $22.50.
Japanese importers have finished buying U.S. soybeans for March shipment and are gradually purchasing for April.
Premiums for U.S. soybeans were quoted at between 115 and 120 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT March, trader said.
Excess rains are delaying the harvest of early-cycle soybeans in the Brazilian state of Mato Grosso, raising fears of a delay in February shipments which could clog up ports for several months.

"Some shipments to Europe will be affected by the rain. But soybean deliveries to Japan are to be started from March, and we don't expect serious trouble at the monent," a senior official at a major oil crusher said.

Taiwanese buying of grains and oilseeds is seen sluggish this week ahead of the Chinese New Year. An expected highlight of limited forthcoming business is Hui Shung Group's expected re-tender on Tuesday or Wednesday for a combined shipment of 38,000 tonnes of soybeans and 16,000 tonnes of corn.
In the Philippines, grain importers are expected to be in the market for rice, corn and wheat this week if international prices fall to lower levels, local traders said.
